name: Pheromone cologne

lead: Pheromone colognes are fragrances or sprays marketed as containing human sex pheromones, with the promise of a more appealing presence and more attention from others. Buyers wear them as a scent-based add-on to grooming and presentation.

The idea draws on research into compounds such as androstenone and androstadienone, which come from sweat glands and are proposed to act through the vomeronasal organ or olfactory receptors. A widely cited encyclopedia summary says no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behavior, and the human vomeronasal organ is described as vestigial in adults.

paras: People wear them like any cologne or body spray, applied after showering and usually alongside regular grooming and a normal fragrance routine. Any effect users notice is typically judged by how others react in social settings.

Reported direct risks are those of any fragrance product, such as skin irritation or allergy in some users. Reviewers note that the attraction effect advertised by sellers is not demonstrated in peer-reviewed work.

forums.title: Does Your Sweat Turn Women On?

angle.text: Buyers wear these scents hoping the added pheromones make them more attractive and give them a more appealing presence, as a fragrance add-on to grooming. Reviewers report that no human pheromone has been shown to change behavior in a peer-reviewed study.

lead: Pheromone cologne is a fragrance or body spray sold with the claim that it contains human pheromones that make the wearer more attractive. Buyers use it as a scent layer on top of grooming, hoping it boosts how appealing they come across, particularly to women; marketing phrases such as 'increase attractiveness' and 'irresistible scent' are common [1][1]. In looksmaxxing circles scent is treated as one more part of presentation, and Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing mentions offshoots such as smellmaxxing [2].

The compounds typically named in products are steroid-like molecules from sweat and other secretions: androstadienone, androstenone, androstenol and estratetraenol [1]. The word 'pheromone' was coined in 1959 [3]. A 1978 study (Kirk-Smith) had people wearing masks treated with androstenol rate photographed faces as warmer and more friendly, and later studies examined mood and attention effects of androstadienone [3]. Wikipedia reports that the field has been marked by small samples, publication bias and weak methods, and that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behaviour, a statement the page marks as disputed [3].

Grokipedia notes that benefits users perceive are widely attributed to placebo effects or to the pleasant qualities of the fragrance itself, and that pheromone colognes follow standard eau-de-cologne construction with alcohol, fixatives and musk, amber, woody or vanilla base notes [1].

paras: Wikipedia describes candidate human compounds including androstenol (1978 photo-rating study), androstenone (1983 skin-conductance changes reported by Van Toller and colleagues) and androstadienone, linked in some experiments to mood and attention to emotional faces [3]. Martha McClintock's 1971 report of menstrual synchrony was later questioned by reviewers, including Strassmann in 1999 and Yang and Schank in 2006 [3]. A 2019 study by Oren and colleagues reported that a putative pheromone affected men's sexual cognition [3].

The human vomeronasal organ, the structure many animals use to detect pheromones, appears atrophied or absent in adults and its receptor genes are nonfunctional, so whether humans detect pheromones through it is disputed [3]. Studying the subject is complicated because participants must be clean and odourless [3].

Grokipedia lists androstadienone for men's products, androstenone, androstenol and estratetraenol as typical ingredients, used at low concentrations in conventional fragrance bases [1]. It names RawChemistry For Him as a top-selling pheromone cologne on Amazon in early 2026 and Bad Wolf and A314 as niche options popular with enthusiasts [1].

Wikipedia reports some body-spray advertisers claim their products contain human sexual pheromones that act as aphrodisiacs [3]. Civetone, a musky compound sourced from civet oil and used as a perfume fixative, is sometimes called a pheromone for animals, and field biologists have used a cologne containing it to attract jaguars to camera traps [4].

Older T Nation threads from 2001 to 2003 ask whether pheromone colognes work; one poster using a pheromone-labelled cologne said it was hard to tell whether it worked and that women did not 'drop at my feet' [5], and another asked about androstenone-based products and their results [6]. A 2002 thread discusses an ingredient list resembling androstenone, androsterone and androstenol [7]. Other posters joke that their natural pheromones are enough [8]. A 2024 psychology-thread poster recalled an old study in which men told they wore an aphrodisiac cologne reported better success with women, which they framed as a confidence effect [9].

No studies found testing commercial pheromone colognes for attractiveness outcomes. Laboratory studies of individual compounds such as androstadienone and androstenol have examined mood, attention and photo ratings in small groups, with variable results [3].

lore.intro: On T Nation, pheromone cologne is discussed from the early 2000s on, usually with curiosity about whether it works and often with jokes about natural musk [5][6][8].
